article_blocks.text: Strain Type: Balanced hybrid
Genetics: Mountaintop Mint #1 × OG Kush × Haze
Breeder: Humboldt Seed Company
THC Content: 25%
CBD Content: N/A
Terpene Profile: N/A
Primary Flavors: Mint, earthy Kush, herbs, pine, mild citrus
Flowering Time (Indoor): 55–60 days
Outdoor Harvest Time: mid-October
Indoor Yield: Medium
Outdoor Yield: Medium
Grow Difficulty: Easy to intermediate

Cob Salad has one of the stranger names in Humboldt Seed Company’s catalog, but its personality is much more deliberate than the name suggests. The cultivar emerged after a lengthy selection process aimed at finding a balanced plant that could combine the cool aromatic character of Mountaintop Mint with the earthy depth of OG Kush and the elevated mental character of Haze. The finished flower leans heavily into mint and fresh herbal aromas, with pine, earth, subtle citrus, and spicy resin filling out the background. It smells cleaner and greener than a typical dessert hybrid, yet the Kush influence keeps it from becoming thin or purely floral.

Humboldt describes the experience as settled and focused while retaining an uplifting sense of mental space. That balance is central to the strain’s identity. Rather than pushing hard toward either sedation or frantic stimulation, the high tends to occupy a more even middle ground. A relatively quick 55–60 day flowering period adds practical appeal, while mold resistance and a mid-October outdoor finish make the plant more versatile than many hybrids carrying noticeable Haze influence.
Genetics and Lineage

Humboldt Seed Company lists the pedigree as Mountaintop Mint #1 × OG Kush × Haze. The breeder does not specify the precise grouping of that three-part formula, so it is best treated exactly as published rather than rearranged into an assumed two-stage cross. Mountaintop Mint #1 provides the most recognizable aromatic contribution, bringing the pronounced mint character that Humboldt emphasizes in descriptions of the finished buds. That parent also contributes modern resin production and a cleaner, fresher aromatic direction than classic Kush alone would provide.

OG Kush introduces the deeper side of the profile. Earth, pine, resin, herbal pungency, and physical relaxation are all consistent with its influence, while Haze brings more vertical energy to both the plant and the experience. Haze ancestry is historically associated with cerebral effects, spice, incense-like complexity, and vigorous growth, although Cob Salad finishes considerably faster than a traditional long-flowering Haze. The combination gives the cultivar enough mental brightness to feel lively while preserving the grounded qualities expected from OG-influenced cannabis .

The breeding objective appears to have centered on balance rather than exaggerating a single parental trait. Mint remains obvious, but it does not erase the earthier Kush foundation. Likewise, Haze influence can add mental lift without turning the plant into a difficult, twelve-week tropical sativa. That middle-ground expression is why Humboldt presents Cob Salad as a balanced hybrid rather than forcing it into a heavily indica- or sativa-dominant category.
Effects and Experience

The first part of the experience tends to feel mentally organized rather than overpowering. Humboldt describes the cultivar as creating a settled and focused feeling, and that characterization fits a hybrid that can lift mood without immediately sending thoughts in too many directions. Familiar tasks may feel more interesting, conversation can become easier, and sensory details such as music or outdoor surroundings may become more noticeable. The effect is cerebral, but usually not as aggressive as a very stimulating Haze.

Physical relaxation develops underneath the clearer mental component. The body may feel calmer and less tense without becoming excessively heavy, particularly at moderate amounts. That balance can make the strain suitable for relaxed daytime or early-evening use for experienced consumers. Higher servings may tilt the experience toward deeper relaxation and reduced motivation, especially in phenotypes expressing more of the OG side.

Because Humboldt does not publish a universal THC percentage, potency should be evaluated from the actual batch rather than assumed from the strain name. Strong cannabis can produce anxiety, dizziness, short-term memory disruption, dry mouth, or impaired coordination when overconsumed. The cultivar’s reputation for focus should also not be interpreted as improved objective performance; even a mentally clear marijuana high can still impair judgment and reaction time.
Medical Benefits

A relatively even combination of mental calm and physical relaxation may appeal to some medical marijuana consumers who dislike strains that immediately become sedating. Cannabis with a similar subjective profile is sometimes selected by people dealing with physical discomfort, appetite changes, or difficulty relaxing while still wanting to remain conversational and mentally engaged. The strain’s balanced character may feel easier to manage than heavily sedating weed during periods when complete inactivity is undesirable.

Cob Salad itself has not been evaluated in controlled clinical trials as a treatment for pain, anxiety, depression, ADHD, insomnia, or another medical condition. Broader research involving cannabis and cannabinoids suggests possible benefits for certain forms of chronic pain and nausea, but those findings involve specific patient populations, doses, and formulations. They should not be automatically transferred to a variable flower cannabis strain simply because its effects are described as relaxing or focused.

THC-rich cannabis may also produce unwanted medical effects. Anxiety can increase in sensitive individuals, coordination and memory may be impaired, and cannabis can interact with some medications. Anyone considering therapeutic use should pay attention to the actual cannabinoid analysis of the flower, begin conservatively, and use appropriate medical guidance when health conditions or prescription drugs are involved.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Mint is the defining aromatic feature. Breaking apart a mature flower can release a cool herbal impression that sits somewhere between fresh mint leaves, green herbs, and resinous vegetation rather than artificial peppermint candy. Beneath that fresher top note is a heavier layer of earth and pine that reflects the OG Kush side of the lineage. Depending on phenotype, subtle citrus or dry Haze spice may also become noticeable after the initial mint begins to fade.

The flavor is generally more complex than the name suggests. Mint and herbal resin can dominate the inhale, followed by earthy Kush, pine, and a slightly spicy finish. Some plants may show a brighter citrus edge, while others lean toward wood, incense, or deeper soil-like notes. The overall profile is less sweet than many modern California hybrids and feels closer to fresh herbs and traditional cannabis resin than to candy or baked goods.

Humboldt does not publish one universal laboratory terpene panel for Cob Salad. Secondary listings sometimes assign specific compounds, but without a breeder-backed batch analysis those profiles should not be treated as permanent characteristics of the strain. The most defensible description remains the breeder’s own emphasis on pronounced mintiness combined with the likely aromatic influence of Kush and Haze ancestry. Proper drying and curing are especially important because the fresher mint and herbal notes can be lost quickly if flowers are exposed to excessive heat.
Growing Information

Cob Salad combines a manageable flowering cycle with genetics capable of showing both hybrid vigor and useful environmental resistance. Humboldt lists approximately 55–60 days from the beginning of flowering to harvest indoors, placing the cultivar comfortably below nine weeks. That speed is notable given the inclusion of Haze genetics, which frequently extend flowering in other hybrids. The plant’s balanced background generally supports moderate branching and a structure that can be managed without the extreme stretch associated with pure tropical sativas.

Mold resistance is one of the breeder-highlighted cultivation traits. That characteristic makes the plant particularly relevant to outdoor gardens or environments where humidity becomes difficult to control late in the season. Resistance should not be interpreted as immunity, however. Adequate spacing, good air circulation, and attention to moisture around developing flowers remain important for maintaining quality. Indoors, the relatively short cycle allows growers to work with a predictable schedule while still taking advantage of the strain’s vigorous hybrid growth.

Outdoor plants are expected to finish around mid-October in suitable Northern Hemisphere climates. Humboldt does not publish fixed indoor grams-per-square-meter or outdoor grams-per-plant figures, so exact yield claims would be speculative. Final production depends heavily on plant size, vegetative time, light exposure, root volume, climate, nutrition, and phenotype. The better approach is to view the cultivar as a stable, adaptable hybrid rather than attaching an unsupported harvest number to every plant.

Post-harvest handling deserves particular care because the defining mint aroma is relatively delicate. Flowers dried too quickly may retain the earthier notes while losing much of their fresh herbal character. A gradual drying period followed by controlled curing allows the mint, pine, spice, and Kush-like earthiness to separate more clearly, producing a much more expressive final flower than rushed weed.
FAQ
What are the genetics of Cob Salad?
Humboldt Seed Company lists Cob Salad as Mountaintop Mint #1 × OG Kush × Haze. The breeder does not specify a more detailed grouping of those three parental components.
Is Cob Salad indica or sativa?

Humboldt describes the cultivar as a balanced hybrid rather than assigning a strongly dominant indica or sativa classification. Its effects combine mental clarity and uplift with noticeable physical relaxation.
What does Cob Salad taste like?
Mint is the standout characteristic, supported by earthy Kush, herbs, pine, spicy resin, and occasional citrus or Haze-like notes.
How long does Cob Salad take to flower?
Indoor flowering takes approximately 55–60 days. Outdoors, plants generally reach harvest around the middle of October in suitable Northern Hemisphere climates.
Is Cob Salad easy to grow?

The strain is relatively approachable because of its short flowering period, balanced hybrid structure, and breeder-highlighted mold resistance. Growers should still maintain good airflow and appropriate humidity around maturing flowers.
Final Thoughts on Cob Salad

Cob Salad stands apart from sweeter modern hybrids by emphasizing fresh herbs, mint, Kush earthiness, and Haze complexity instead of candy or dessert flavors. Mountaintop Mint #1 establishes the aromatic signature, while OG Kush and Haze broaden both the plant’s structure and the experience. The result feels contemporary without abandoning the traditional pine, earth, and resin character that defines much of classic cannabis.

Its cultivation profile is equally balanced. A 55–60 day indoor flowering period keeps turnaround relatively fast, mold resistance improves adaptability, and the mid-October outdoor finish remains manageable in many suitable climates. Humboldt’s decision not to attach universal yield or THC numbers to the line also avoids implying a level of precision that seed-grown cannabis cannot consistently provide.

The effect completes the concept. Cob Salad can feel mentally lifted and settled at the same time, with physical relaxation developing underneath rather than immediately overwhelming the experience. That combination of mint-heavy aroma, balanced effects, useful resistance, and manageable flowering time gives the cultivar a clear identity despite its unconventional name.
